1.title: The AWS Cloud: Value, Reach and Economics
1.text: Welcome to Module one: the A W S Cloud, its value, its reach, and its economics. This module opens the first domain of the exam, Cloud Concepts, which is twenty-four percent of scored content. It covers task statements one point one and one point four: the benefits of the cloud, and the concepts of cloud economics.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Define cloud computing, and tell the service models apart. Name the six advantages of the A W S Cloud, and match each to a situation. Explain speed, global reach, high availability and elasticity. Compare fixed and variable cost, and the costs of running your own data center. And describe licensing options, rightsizing and automation as ways to control cost.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater Weighs Its Server Room
1.text: Tidewater Outfitters rents a small server room that runs its online shop. Sales triple at the holidays and then fall, yet the servers are sized for the peak all year. Buying more hardware takes weeks, and new customers in Europe see slow pages. The finance lead also owns Windows Server licenses and wants to keep using them. Your job is to explain what moving to A W S would change, in benefits and in cost.

1.title: What Is Cloud Computing?
1.text: Start with the definition. Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of I T resources over the internet, with pay-as-you-go pricing. Instead of owning servers and data centers, you use computing, storage and databases from a provider such as A W S. You pay for what you use, and you can stop when you no longer need a resource. The provider takes care of the facilities, the hardware and the power, and you choose and use the services. Exam tip: on demand, plus pay as you go, is the core definition.

1.title: Service Models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
1.text: This slide goes beyond the exam guide, but it helps with vocabulary. There are three service models. Infrastructure as a Service, I A A S, gives you the basic building blocks of networking, compute and storage, with the most control. Platform as a Service, P A A S, removes the need to manage the underlying infrastructure, so you can focus on your application. Software as a Service, S A A S, is a complete product that the provider runs and manages, such as web-based email. As you go from I A A S to S A A S, you manage less and the provider manages more. Exam tip: more control means more to manage.

1.title: The Value Proposition: Six Advantages
1.text: A W S describes the value of the cloud as six advantages. First, trade fixed expense for variable expense: you pay only when you consume. Second, benefit from massive economies of scale, which gives a lower variable cost than you could get on your own. Third, stop guessing capacity, and scale up and down as required. Fourth, increase speed and agility, with resources in minutes instead of weeks. Fifth, stop spending money running and maintaining data centers, and focus on your business. And sixth, go global in minutes, by deploying in several Regions with a few clicks. Exam tip: know all six, because questions often describe one in different words.

1.title: Speed of Deployment and Agility
1.text: Take speed first. In the cloud, new I T resources are a click away, so the wait for developers falls from weeks to minutes. Because experimenting costs less money and less time, the organization becomes more agile. Teams can try different instance types, storage or setups quickly, and drop whatever does not work. For Tidewater, a new test environment for the holiday sale is ready the same day, not after a hardware order. Exam tip: speed of deployment means minutes instead of weeks, and agility means the cost of trying things is low.

1.title: Global Reach in Minutes
1.text: Next, global reach. With the A W S global infrastructure, you can deploy an application in several Regions around the world with a few clicks. Customers then connect to resources close to them, which gives lower latency and a better experience. It costs little extra to reach new markets, because you do not build new data centers. For Tidewater, a second Region near Europe makes the shop faster for European customers. Regions and Availability Zones are covered in Module six. Exam tip: global reach is about deploying close to customers, and lower latency is the benefit to remember.

1.title: High Availability
1.text: High availability means a workload keeps running when part of it fails. The idea is to use several smaller resources and spread requests across them, so they do not share one point of failure. Look at the picture. A load balancer sends customers to two servers in separate locations. One location fails, and the other keeps serving. A W S design guidance adds three habits: monitor, recover automatically, and test your recovery. And A W S builds its infrastructure from Regions and Availability Zones, so you can spread a workload across locations. Exam tip: for keeps working after a failure, think high availability.

1.title: Elasticity: Capacity That Follows Demand
1.text: Elasticity means adding and removing resources as demand changes. On premises, you buy for the peak, and the extra capacity sits idle the rest of the time. Look at the two panels. On the left, fixed capacity is set at the peak. On the right, elastic capacity rises and falls with demand. In the cloud you stop guessing capacity: you scale up and down with a few minutes' notice. Both risks go away, the expensive idle resources and too little capacity. Auto scaling is the A W S feature behind it, and Module seven covers it. Exam tip: elasticity works in both directions.

1.title: Which Benefit Is It?
1.text: Let us practice matching benefits to situations. A test environment ready in minutes, not weeks, is speed and agility. Extra servers for the holiday sale, removed afterwards, is elasticity. European customers served from a nearby Region is global reach. A shop that stays up when one location fails is high availability. Paying per use instead of buying servers first is trading fixed expense for variable expense. And lower prices because many customers share the cost is economies of scale. Exam tip: find the key phrase. Minutes means speed, both directions means elasticity, and close to customers means global reach.

1.title: Fixed Costs and Variable Costs
1.text: Now cloud economics. Fixed expense means you invest in data centers and servers before you know how you will use them. Variable expense means you pay only when you consume resources, and only for how much you consume. A W S gives an example of adopting a consumption model. A development environment used eight hours a day on weekdays can be stopped when it is idle. A W S puts the savings at about seventy-five percent, which is forty hours against one hundred sixty-eight. Variable cost also lowers the risk of buying too much or too little. Exam tip: trade fixed expense for variable expense means pay for what you use instead of buying capacity first.

1.title: Costs of Running Your Own Data Center
1.text: What does running your own data center cost? It means procurement, which is buying and waiting, plus maintenance and capacity planning. It also means the heavy lifting: racking, stacking and powering servers, and managing operating systems and applications. A W S does the data center work, and managed services remove much of the operating burden. That effort moves from running infrastructure to using services and serving customers. You still pay for the services you use, and for the people who design and run your workloads. Exam tip: on-premises costs are more than hardware. Add buying, upkeep, power, space and staff time.

1.title: Economies of Scale
1.text: Economies of scale are one of the six advantages. Usage from hundreds of thousands of customers is aggregated in the cloud. That lets A W S achieve higher economies of scale, and they become lower pay-as-you-go prices. So you can reach a lower variable cost than you could on your own. For Tidewater, a small shop gets prices built on the volume of a very large provider. Prices still differ by Region and service, and Module thirteen covers them. Exam tip: many customers share the cost, so each pays less per unit.

1.title: Licensing: Bring Your Own License or License Included
1.text: The exam guide names two licensing strategies. With Bring Your Own License, called B Y O L, you reuse licenses you already own on A W S, which can save cost. With an included license, the license cost is part of the price of the A W S resource. B Y O L means you follow the vendor's license terms and track usage, while an included license is simpler. A W S License Manager can switch a workload between the two license types without redeploying it. Exam tip: B Y O L means you bring a license you own; included means the license is already in the price.

2.title: AWS License Manager
2.text: A W S License Manager manages software licenses from vendors such as Microsoft, S A P, Oracle and I B M. It works across Regions and accounts, and gives dashboards for usage and for vendor audits. Rule-based limits, hard or soft, stop non-compliant use before it happens. It tracks software licensed by virtual cores, physical cores, sockets or machines. And it integrates with Amazon E C two, Amazon R D S, A W S Marketplace, Systems Manager and A W S Organizations. Exam tip: tracking licenses and staying compliant on A W S is License Manager.

2.title: Rightsizing: Matching Size to Workload
2.text: Rightsizing is matching instance types and sizes to your workload. A W S calls it the most effective way to control cloud costs. Look at the three servers. One is too large and mostly idle, which wastes money. One is right-sized and fits the workload. One is too small and overflowing, which hurts performance. Migrated workloads are often oversized, because speed came before cost. So review usage continuously, shut down idle resources, and resize overprovisioned ones. Needs change, so treat rightsizing as ongoing. Exam tip: too big wastes money, and too small hurts performance.

2.title: Tools That Help: Compute Optimizer and Cost Explorer
2.text: Two tools help here. A W S Compute Optimizer gives recommendations that show where an instance can be resized. A W S Cost Explorer helps you analyze costs and usage over time. Tags let you assign cost to teams and workloads, so waste has an owner. A W S suggests a rightsizing schedule for each team, and tagging every instance. Pricing and billing tools are covered in Module thirteen. Exam tip: resize recommendations, Compute Optimizer. Looking at past spend, Cost Explorer.

2.title: Automation: Faster, Repeatable, Less Error-Prone
2.text: The exam guide also asks for the benefits of automation. A W S design guidance says to perform operations as code, so procedures are versioned, tested and automated. It says to manage change through automation, and to recover from failure automatically. Automation can add or remove resources to match demand, which supports elasticity. Fewer manual steps mean faster, more repeatable work, and fewer mistakes. And experimenting with different configurations becomes cheap when resources can be automated. Exam tip: benefits of automation are speed, consistency and less manual effort.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Value and Economics
2.text: Here are the look-alike pairs for this module. Elasticity or high availability: capacity follows demand, or the workload survives failure. Agility or global reach: speed of change, or closeness to customers. Fixed or variable expense: pay first, or pay as you use. B Y O L or included license: a license you own, or one in the price. Compute Optimizer or Cost Explorer: resize advice, or spend analysis. And I A A S, P A A S or S A A S: how much you manage. Exam tip: name the situation first, then the benefit.

2.title: Design Check: Tidewater's Move
2.text: Time to design. Look at Tidewater's six situations, and answer each one yourself before I do. Holiday spikes with idle capacity the rest of the year call for elasticity: scale up and down and pay for use. Buying servers before knowing demand is the shift from fixed to variable expense. New customers in Europe and Asia call for global reach: deploy in more Regions. Windows Server licenses already owned mean Bring Your Own License, tracked with License Manager. Servers that are oversized after the move need rightsizing with Compute Optimizer. And release steps repeated by hand call for automation, with operations as code.

2.title: Common Traps: Value and Economics
2.text: Watch for five traps. Elasticity is not high availability: one changes capacity with demand, the other survives failure. Variable expense is not always cheaper, because pay-per-use rewards stopping and rightsizing resources. Agility is about speed of change, not uptime. B Y O L is not automatic: it depends on the vendor's license terms. And more control means more to manage, so I A A S gives the most control and the most work. Exam tip: if two answers both sound good, check which one matches the exact benefit in the question.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. Cloud computing is on-demand I T resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing, and the service models differ in what you manage. The six advantages are variable expense, economies of scale, no capacity guessing, speed and agility, no data center upkeep, and global reach. High availability avoids single points of failure, and elasticity adds and removes capacity. Fixed expense is paid first and variable expense follows use, and your own data center adds buying, upkeep and staff. B Y O L reuses licenses you own, an included license is in the price, and License Manager tracks them. And for cost control: rightsize with Compute Optimizer, analyze with Cost Explorer, and automate.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Which statement best describes cloud computing? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of I T resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. Owning servers, a fixed multi-year contract and a purely private network describe traditional approaches.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A team can launch a new test environment in minutes instead of waiting weeks for hardware. Which cloud benefit does this describe? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A, increased speed and agility. Economies of scale are about lower prices, global reach is about deploying near customers, and high availability is about surviving failures.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Tidewater's traffic triples at the holidays and then falls. Which cloud benefit lets the shop add capacity for the season and release it afterwards? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D, elasticity. It adds and removes resources as demand changes, so the shop pays for the extra capacity only while it needs it.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. Select two. Which two are advantages of cloud computing? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C: trading fixed expense for variable expense, and increasing speed and agility. The cloud does not guarantee lower cost for every workload, does not remove your own security duties, and does not remove the need to think about capacity.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Which description best fits high availability? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B, a workload that keeps running when part of it fails. High availability usually means spreading work across several resources with no single point of failure. Growing automatically is elasticity, and the lowest cost is cost optimization.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Which statement describes a variable expense? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. You pay only for the resources you consume, in the amount you consume. Paying a large amount up front, paying a flat amount whether or not you use the resources, and buying equipment outright are fixed expenses.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Tidewater already owns Windows Server licenses and wants to reuse them on A W S to save cost. Which approach fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B, Bring Your Own License. It lets a company reuse licenses it already owns, subject to the vendor's terms. Included licenses charge for a license it does not need.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. After the move, Tidewater's servers run at about ten percent C P U use. Which practice reduces cost without losing the capacity the shop needs? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C, rightsizing. It matches instance sizes to what the workload really uses, so idle capacity stops costing money. Larger or additional instances raise cost, and turning off monitoring removes the information you need.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. Select two. Which two A W S tools help you find and act on rightsizing and spending opportunities? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D: Compute Optimizer recommends where instances can be resized, and Cost Explorer lets you analyze costs and usage. Cognito handles app sign-in, Secrets Manager stores secrets, and Artifact provides compliance reports.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. Which statement about economies of scale in the cloud is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Aggregated usage from many customers lets A W S offer lower pay-as-you-go prices. The other statements deny that effect, or reverse it.

2.title: Practice Question 11
2.text: Question eleven. Tidewater runs a development environment only during an eight-hour working day. Which action best applies the consumption model? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: stop the environment when it is not in use, so it runs only when needed. Running around the clock, buying larger instances, or adding a second Region all increase what you pay.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all eleven answers. Question one: C. Question two: A. Question three: D. Question four: A and C. Question five: B. Question six: A. Question seven: B. Question eight: C. Question nine: B and D. Question ten: D. Question eleven: A. That completes Module one. Next, Module two covers the Well-Architected Framework, cloud adoption, and migration.
